<reason>Both sides argued well and the clash was genuine. PRO's strongest asset was its framing (hidden vs. visible increases; shrinkflation only works because it hides) and its inattention dichotomy. But CON answered that dichotomy directly ("attention is scarce, not zero" — one salient number at the point of decision versus a second competing sticker), and PRO's closing simply repeated the dichotomy rather than engaging that answer. CON also tracked the mandate's growth from "a line of code" to "substantially similar" adjudication across SKUs, and turned PRO's own A2 answer ("switches, buys the competitor") into the charge that the flag steers shoppers away from what may still be the best per-gram value. PRO's reply that resentment is "the market's own sanction" has real force as a dynamic-discipline argument, and CON never fully addressed that dynamic, which keeps this close. PRO also suffered more execution cost with four clipped turns including a lost opening conclusion. On balance CON's rebuttals were more surgical and adapted better to the evolving exchange, giving it a razor-thin edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 A1/A2 and weighing: it dissolved PRO's inattention dichotomy ("scarce, not zero"; consolidate the one decisive number rather than dilute it), then used PRO's own [A4.3] admission that the flag's purpose is to make shoppers switch to argue this produces worse purchases when the shrunk brand remains cheaper per gram, while cataloguing how the "line of code" had become a compliance regime.</best_rebuttal>
